title: The Seven Conditions of the Vajjis
text:
King Ajatasattu of Magadha wanted to conquer the Vajjis, a confederation of clans ruled by assemblies rather than a single king. Before marching, he sent his chief minister, Vassakara, to the Buddha to ask what the outcome would be.

The Buddha did not answer the minister directly. He turned to Ananda, who was fanning him, and asked a series of questions. Did the Vajjis meet often and in full numbers? Did they meet in harmony, end their meetings in harmony and carry out their business in harmony? Did they keep to their established laws rather than inventing new ones on a whim? Did they honor and listen to their elders, protect their women, maintain their shrines, and look after holy men who came to them? To each question Ananda answered yes.

As long as the Vajjis kept to these seven things, the Buddha said, they could be expected to prosper and not decline. Vassakara drew the conclusion himself: the Vajjis could not be beaten in war, except through bribery or by breaking up their unity. Then he left. The Buddha later gathered his monks and applied the same conditions to their own community.
lesson: Groups that meet regularly, decide together and carry out decisions in unity are hard to defeat. Watch for the first signs of division, because that is where outsiders get in.
people: The Buddha, Ananda, the minister Vassakara, King Ajatasattu
